title: What is a money laundering reporting officer (MLRO)?
description: An MLRO receives internal suspicion reports and decides what goes to the FIU. How MLRO and AML compliance officer roles vary across markets.
shortAnswer: A money laundering reporting officer (MLRO) is the individual in a regulated business who receives internal reports of suspected money laundering or terrorist financing, decides whether to report them to the national financial intelligence unit, and usually oversees the anti-money laundering program, including staff training. Many markets call the role the AML compliance officer or BSA officer instead, and some split reporting and program oversight between two people.
keyTakeaways: Almost every AML regime requires a named person responsible for AML compliance; the title MLRO is used in some markets, AML compliance officer or BSA officer in others.
In the Dubai International Financial Centre, the MLRO is a mandatory appointment held by an approved Authorised Individual with at least 15 hours of continuing professional development a year.
The EU Anti-Money Laundering Regulation, applying from 10 July 2027, requires both a compliance manager on the management body and a compliance officer.
The role commonly owns or approves AML training content, so training records are part of its evidence.
The MLRO needs deeper training than other staff because they make the reporting decision.

sections.heading: What does a money laundering reporting officer do?

blocks.text: An MLRO receives and assesses internal suspicious activity reports and decides which to file with the financial intelligence unit, and in most firms also runs or oversees the anti-money laundering and counter terrorist financing (AML/CFT) program. Typical duties include:

items: Receiving internal reports from staff and deciding whether to file a suspicious transaction or activity report.
Acting as the contact point for the financial intelligence unit and the supervisor.
Maintaining AML/CFT policies, procedures and the business wide risk assessment.
Developing, approving or delivering AML/CFT training, and reporting on completion and effectiveness.
Reporting to senior management or the board on the program.

sections.heading: How does the role differ across markets?

blocks.text: Every major AML regime requires a designated person, but the title, seniority, approval and training rules differ. The table gives examples from five markets.

In Australia, the AML/CTF reforms required existing reporting entities to notify AUSTRAC of their compliance officer by 30 May 2026.

sections.heading: What training does an MLRO need?

blocks.text: An MLRO needs training deep enough to make defensible reporting decisions and to run the program, which goes well beyond general staff awareness. Regulators signal this in different ways: the [DFSA](/regulations/dfsa-training-and-competence-requirements) sets a minimum number of CPD hours, and AUSTRAC's [training guidance](https://www.austrac.gov.au/industry-and-business/obligations-and-guidance/your-amlctf-program/personnel-due-diligence-and-training/amlctf-training) gives example refresh intervals of 6 to 12 months for compliance officers and senior management, while noting these are examples only.

A practical MLRO curriculum covers the legal reporting tests and timing, typologies relevant to the firm's products, the national risk assessment, sanctions screening, tipping off rules, investigation and documentation of decisions, and how to evaluate training effectiveness for others. The country requirements are compared in [AML training requirements by country](/compare/aml-training-requirements-by-country).

sections.heading: Why is the MLRO usually the owner of AML training?

blocks.text: Because several regimes give the AML officer explicit training duties, the MLRO is the natural owner of the training program's content. UAE Cabinet Resolution No. 134 of 2025 makes training plans a compliance officer duty, Portugal's Law 83/2017 requires a prior favorable opinion of the compliance officer on training, and the [EU AMLR](/regulations/eu-amlr-training-requirements) has the compliance officer approve the content of employee assessments. The L&D team usually owns delivery and records, while the MLRO signs off role based outcomes; see [know your customer](/glossary/know-your-customer) for the frontline content that sits underneath.

sections.heading: How does Knowledge Foundry approach this?

blocks.text: Knowledge Foundry gives the MLRO a structured view of AML/CFT obligations mapped to role based competencies and assessments, with each requirement linked to its source. The MLRO approves outcomes once, and changes to the law or risk assessment show which roles and assessments need updating.

faqs.q: Is the MLRO the same as the AML compliance officer?
faqs.a: Often, but not always. In many firms one person does both. Some regimes or larger firms separate the reporting function from program oversight, or add a senior management accountable role above them, as the EU AMLR does with its compliance manager on the management body.

faqs.q: Does the MLRO need to be approved by the regulator?
faqs.a: It depends on the market. In the DIFC the MLRO must be a DFSA approved Authorised Individual, and UAE federal supervisors may require prior approval of compliance officer appointments. In the United States, the institution designates the person without a regulatory approval step.

faqs.q: Can the MLRO role be outsourced?
faqs.a: Rules vary, and some regimes require a management level appointment, as UAE federal rules do for the compliance officer. Even where operational tasks can be outsourced, responsibility for compliance stays with the regulated firm. Check the specific rule and the supervisor's guidance before outsourcing.

Usually external providers, professional bodies and the firm's own legal or compliance specialists. The firm should still record what the MLRO completed and how it relates to the role's obligations, because supervisors may review the MLRO's competence along with staff training.
